title: Rescue the local startup
intro: Fieldstore will not start. Inspect each synthetic terminal clue and choose the smallest repair. No commands are executed by this mission.

scenarios.title: A command in the parent folder
evidence: Working directory: projects/
Application files: projects/fieldstore/package.json
npm run dev: ENOENT, package.json not found
scenarios.question: What should you check or change first?

choices.text: Enter the verified fieldstore application directory and inspect its scripts.
choices.why: The command is resolving files from the wrong directory; locating the actual package is the direct repair.

choices.text: Delete the lockfile and upgrade all packages.
choices.why: Dependency updates cannot make a command read the intended package from the wrong folder.

choices.text: Create a hosted database.
choices.why: No backend service is involved in this local file-location error.

scenarios.title: The executable is missing
evidence: Working directory contains the intended package.json and package-lock.json.
The dev script invokes next.
npm ls reports missing declared dependencies; no successful install is recorded.
scenarios.question: Which next step fits this evidence?

choices.text: Disable all server permission checks.
choices.why: Permission checks do not install the declared development executable.

choices.text: Verify runtime and manifest/lock agreement, then run the intended lockfile install.
choices.why: The package definition exists but the installation is missing; check compatibility before installing its locked tree.

choices.text: Change port numbers until next appears.
choices.why: A port change cannot supply an absent dependency.

scenarios.title: The local address is occupied
evidence: Dependencies are installed.
Startup reports EADDRINUSE on127.0.0.1:3000.
Another known local development process is already listening there.
scenarios.question: What is an appropriate resolution?

choices.text: Assume the product schema is invalid.
choices.why: The failure occurs while binding an address, before a product query.

choices.text: Terminate every process on the computer.
choices.why: That is unrelated and unnecessarily disruptive; identify the actual listener.

choices.text: Inspect the existing listener, then stop it deliberately or use a different local port.
choices.why: One address/port cannot be owned by two listening processes; resolve the specific conflict.

completion: You can identify directory, installation, and binding failures without changing unrelated code or creating cloud resources.

title: Repair the configuration boundary
intro: Sort each described item by intended destination, then repair the simulated configuration. All displayed values are synthetic; an example-placeholder is nonfunctional documentation, not a credential.

sortItems.label: NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL: selected project's public URL
sortItems.why: The public endpoint identifies the project; it is deliberately visible and is not a customer identity.

sortItems.label: NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY: actual publishable application key
sortItems.why: This key is designed for public components; grants, RLS, and user identity still determine access.

sortItems.label: SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY: actual privileged credential
sortItems.why: It bypasses RLS and must stay in controlled backend consumers.

sortItems.label: DATABASE_URL: actual connection string with database password
sortItems.why: A database credential is not public SDK configuration.

sortItems.label: PAYMENT_WEBHOOK_SECRET: actual verification secret
sortItems.why: Incoming event verification material belongs on the receiving backend.

sortItems.label: .env.example: DATABASE_URL=replace-with-local-test-url
sortItems.why: This documents a required name with a deliberately nonfunctional value.

sortItems.label: .env.example: SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY=replace-only-on-server
sortItems.why: A placeholder is documentation; no real secret belongs in the committed template.

sortItems.label: NEXT_PUBLIC_STORE_NAME: Fieldstore
sortItems.why: A public display label is intentionally inspectable and carries no privileged access.

scenarios.title: Testing points at production
evidence: FIELDSTORE_ENV=test
Effective DATABASE_URL target is classified production.
A shell environment override takes precedence over local files.
scenarios.question: What should happen before any test seed or write?

choices.text: Run once to see whether important rows change.
choices.why: The target is already known to be forbidden; a trial write can damage real data.

choices.text: Refuse startup, repair the complete target/credential bundle, and validate isolation.
choices.why: The effective target determines impact, regardless of a test label.

choices.text: Rename DATABASE_URL without changing its value.
choices.why: A new name does not change where a connection goes.

scenarios.title: A public privileged key
evidence: A developer added NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY.
The client build contains its actual privileged value.
The local file is ignored by Git.
scenarios.question: Which repair addresses exposure and future access?

choices.text: Only delete the local file.
choices.why: Built files and other copies may retain an active credential.

choices.text: Keep it because .gitignore protects browser bundles.
choices.why: .gitignore does not control what a build sends to clients.

choices.text: Remove the exposure, rotate/revoke the key under the incident plan, and update controlled consumers.
choices.why: Fix the code path and the provider-side capability; neither step alone completes recovery.

scenarios.title: A frozen public project URL
evidence: The client artifact was built for a staging target.
A server variable was changed later.
The browser still uses the staged public URL.
scenarios.question: What explains the result?

choices.text: The public value was embedded at build time; rebuild intentionally or design safe runtime configuration.
choices.why: A server environment edit does not rewrite already built JavaScript.

choices.text: All browsers continuously read the server's process.env.
choices.why: The client does not have direct access to server process memory.

choices.text: Prefixing a secret with NEXT_PUBLIC encrypts it.
choices.why: The prefix exposes supported values to the client; it is not encryption.

completion: You can classify capability, refuse cross-environment writes, and distinguish build-time public values from protected runtime credentials.

title: Assemble Add to cart
intro: Order this specific Fieldstore mutation route, then find misplaced checks. This model saves cart intention but does not reserve stock.

orderItems.label: Shopper selects a variant and clicks Add to cart.
orderItems.why: The browser collects an intention, not an authoritative price or identity.

orderItems.label: Browser sends desired variant and quantity to the existing server entry point.
orderItems.why: The request carries untrusted input for validation.

orderItems.label: Server verifies identity, scopes the cart, and validates current rules.
orderItems.why: The actual operation enforces access even when UI controls are bypassed.

orderItems.label: Shared cart operation commits the permitted quantity change.
orderItems.why: Persistent state and defined retry semantics make the result survive refresh without unintended increments.

orderItems.label: Return the authoritative cart or safe error.
orderItems.why: The response reports the actual outcome instead of presuming every click succeeded.

orderItems.label: Browser renders the confirmed result or reconciles provisional UI.
orderItems.why: Presentation follows evidence; it cannot substitute for the saved record.

scenarios.title: Security only in the component
evidence: The admin button is hidden.
The Server Action checks only that any session exists.
A normal customer can call it directly.
scenarios.question: Where is the required repair?

choices.text: Add operation/resource authorization inside the trusted action path.
choices.why: Hidden controls and action identifiers do not enforce server permission.

choices.text: Make the button smaller.
choices.why: Visual design cannot constrain a direct request.

choices.text: Use a more obscure action name.
choices.why: Obscurity is not an authorization policy.

scenarios.title: Two meanings of quantity
evidence: The server increments by2 on each request.
A timeout triggers a retry of the same intended action.
The cart grows by4.
scenarios.question: What must be clarified and protected?

choices.text: The color of the success toast.
choices.why: The stored quantity, not its appearance, is incorrect.

choices.text: Set-versus-increment semantics and repeat-safe operation handling.
choices.why: A repeated request must not unexpectedly repeat the intended effect.

choices.text: Only the page refresh interval.
choices.why: Refreshing will show the wrong persisted quantity rather than repair it.

scenarios.title: Malformed request
evidence: POST body is broken JSON.
The handler returns a raw parser stack trace.
No cart write occurred.
scenarios.question: Which behavior should replace the raw disclosure?

choices.text: Return200 and create an empty order.
choices.why: Malformed input must not become fabricated success or an unrelated mutation.

choices.text: Expose environment values to help the customer debug.
choices.why: That would disclose configuration without solving the input error.

choices.text: Return the documented safe parse error and keep redacted diagnostics server-side.
choices.why: Handle invalid input deliberately, without leaking internals or claiming a write.

completion: You can trace request-to-record behavior and locate permission, retry, and parsing checks in trusted code.

title: Defend two customer accounts
intro: Use a publishable component key and distinct synthetic user identities. Secret-key success is not evidence that customer policies work.

scenarios.title: Customer A selects B's order
evidence: Both users are signed in separately.
The intended SELECT policy checks auth.uid() = customer_id.
A targets B's order ID directly.
scenarios.question: What is the intended customer result?

choices.text: Return B's order because A is authenticated.
choices.why: Authentication alone does not authorize a different customer's resource.

choices.text: No B row becomes visible to A under the ownership policy.
choices.why: The row predicate scopes the otherwise permitted SELECT; the API may represent this as an empty result.

choices.text: Reveal the row but hide the button afterward.
choices.why: The data would already be exposed.

scenarios.title: New table has no API grant
evidence: The table exists and RLS is enabled.
Data API reports permission denied for the intended role.
No appropriate SELECT grant is present.
scenarios.question: Which change addresses the actual access layer?

choices.text: Disable RLS on all tables.
choices.why: Row filtering is separate from the missing operation privilege and should remain enforced.

choices.text: Put the privileged secret key in the browser.
choices.why: That bypasses protection and exposes elevated capability.

choices.text: Review exposure and add only the intended table privilege while retaining appropriate RLS.
choices.why: A grant makes the operation eligible; policies still constrain which rows it can access.

scenarios.title: Own order does not mean editable money
evidence: Customer A may read A's order.
A submits paid=true and total_minor=1.
Order money and payment transitions are server-owned.
scenarios.question: Which result preserves the store's model?

choices.text: Reject the unauthorized mutation even though the customer owns the order.
choices.why: Ownership permits only explicitly allowed operations and fields, not rewriting financial truth.

choices.text: Accept it because any owner may edit any field.
choices.why: That confuses resource scope with operation and column authority.

choices.text: Accept it only when the browser hides the price input.
choices.why: A direct caller can still submit the field; UI visibility adds no permission.

completion: You can distinguish role grants, row scope, operation/column permission, and bypass credentials using direct two-customer tests.

title: Repair the identity journey
intro: Follow three synthetic account incidents without logging tokens, contacting Auth, or creating users.

scenarios.title: A cookie that is no longer enough
evidence: The browser has an expired access token.
Server code trusts the getSession user object.
A protected order read is attempted without verified identity.
scenarios.question: What should the trusted path do?

choices.text: Follow supported refresh, verify identity, and authorize the order; require sign-in if recovery fails.
choices.why: A session-shaped value does not establish current valid identity or order permission.

choices.text: Trust any cookie containing a user ID.
choices.why: Client-controlled storage is not sufficient verification.

choices.text: Disable all order ownership checks while refreshing.
choices.why: Identity renewal does not justify removing resource protection.

scenarios.title: The callback points elsewhere
evidence: Fieldstore runs at127.0.0.1:3000.
The configured callback points to a different hostname.
The login return does not establish the intended local session.
scenarios.question: Which focused repair is appropriate?

choices.text: Allow every possible redirect destination.
choices.why: A broad bypass obscures the configuration error and can enable unsafe redirects.

choices.text: Match the approved exact origin/path and verify the documented exchange and cookie flow.
choices.why: Callback configuration and completion must agree with the actual environment.

choices.text: Store the user's password in the URL.
choices.why: That exposes credentials and does not implement the required exchange.

scenarios.title: The self-awarded admin role
evidence: A customer updates user_metadata.role to admin.
The refund handler reads that field as authority.
No trusted staff assignment exists.
scenarios.question: Which boundary must be restored?

choices.text: Only rename the profile form field.
choices.why: The user can still edit permitted metadata directly.

choices.text: Keep trusting it because it appears in a signed token.
choices.why: A signed claim can still carry user-editable content; signature does not make that content a trusted assignment.

choices.text: Use protected staff assignments and current permission checks where required.
choices.why: Authority must come from a trusted assignment path and account for stale claims.

completion: You can separate session data from verification, exact callback routing, and trusted staff authority.

title: Protect files and recover live updates
intro: Configure the intended access behavior for synthetic Fieldstore photos, invoices, updates, and function work. No bucket, subscription, or function is created.

scenarios.title: Photo versus invoice
evidence: Approved product photos should be publicly visible.
Invoices contain private customer details.
Uploads and deletions still require authorized actors.
scenarios.question: Which bucket/access design fits?

choices.text: Put both file types in one public bucket and use long names.
choices.why: A public invoice remains publicly retrievable when its URL is known.

choices.text: Public approved photos; private invoices with per-document authorization and scoped downloads.
choices.why: Audience determines delivery policy; public retrieval does not require public write privileges.

choices.text: Allow every signed-in user to issue invoice URLs for any path.
choices.why: Being signed in does not establish ownership of a specific document.

scenarios.title: A misleading image upload
evidence: The browser says photo.jpg.
Actual bytes are not an approved image format.
The upload exceeds the configured dimension/size policy.
scenarios.question: What should the workflow do?

choices.text: Publish because the extension is .jpg.
choices.why: The name and claimed content type are untrusted.

choices.text: Make the bucket public to solve validation.
choices.why: Visibility does not inspect bytes or enforce the intended safety limits.

choices.text: Reject or quarantine through the defined inspection path before any public derivative is served.
choices.why: Authorized, bounded, actual-content validation must precede public publication.

scenarios.title: The realtime connection gap
evidence: The dashboard was offline for ten minutes.
Orders may have changed during that interval.
The current socket shows no new event.
scenarios.question: How should the view recover?

choices.text: Reauthorize and refetch current durable state, then restore the scoped subscription.
choices.why: No visible event cannot prove no missed change; current state repairs the knowledge gap.

choices.text: Assume the old screen is complete forever.
choices.why: Disconnected delivery provides no such guarantee.

choices.text: Repeat the customer's payment to generate a fresh event.
choices.why: A new charge is unrelated and unsafe.

scenarios.title: Verified user, privileged query
evidence: An Edge Function verifies a real user.
Its admin client bypasses RLS.
The query selects every customer's invoice record.
scenarios.question: What else is required?

choices.text: Only a nicer success message.
choices.why: The problem is unauthorized data scope.

choices.text: Enforce the caller's resource scope or use a correctly caller-scoped client.
choices.why: Identity verification does not constrain privileged database access by itself.

choices.text: Send the secret key to the browser for filtering.
choices.why: That exposes elevated capability and moves enforcement into an untrusted client.

completion: You can configure public/private file paths, require real upload inspection, recover missed state, and retain authorization inside privileged functions.

title: Repair the simulated preview
intro: Inspect a fictional release of Fieldstore. Choose the change supported by the evidence. Nothing is deployed.

scenarios.title: Green build, broken cart
evidence: Build: passed for rev-PLACEHOLDER
Preview request: CONFIG_MISSING DATABASE_URL
Variable scope: production only
scenarios.question: What is the smallest correct repair?

choices.text: Add an isolated preview configuration and create a new simulated deployment.
choices.why: The preview needs its own scoped value, and deployment configuration is not retroactively rewritten.

choices.text: Use the production database in every environment.
choices.why: This breaks data isolation and can turn testing into real changes.

choices.text: Expose DATABASE_URL to the browser.
choices.why: A database credential must not enter a public bundle.

scenarios.title: Login returns to the wrong host
evidence: Shop host: shop.example.test
Auth callback: old-preview.example.test/auth/callback
Database probe: passed
scenarios.question: Where should you investigate?

choices.text: Delete all auth checks.
choices.why: The evidence points to the return URL contract, not a need to remove verification.

choices.text: Compare the exact approved callback and site URL for this environment.
choices.why: Scheme, host and path must match the intended login flow; update only approved destinations.

choices.text: Buy a larger compute plan.
choices.why: More compute cannot fix the callback mismatch.

scenarios.title: The old browser URL remains
evidence: NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL changed after build
Current browser bundle still contains old.example.test
No new deployment was built
scenarios.question: What explains the result?

choices.text: Public build-time values may remain embedded until a new build.
choices.why: A running environment variable cannot rewrite already-produced JavaScript.

choices.text: The browser can decrypt hidden server secrets.
choices.why: Public variables are intentionally exposed, not encrypted credentials.

choices.text: The database password is necessarily wrong.
choices.why: No database evidence supports that conclusion.

scenarios.title: Rollback and side effects
evidence: rev-B created SHIPMENT_PLACEHOLDER
rev-B then began returning errors
rev-A is considered for rollback
scenarios.question: Which step belongs in recovery?

choices.text: Erase the provider shipment ID.
choices.why: Erasing evidence makes duplicate fulfillment more likely.

choices.text: Assume rollback cancels the parcel.
choices.why: Changing application code does not undo external resources.

choices.text: Check old-code compatibility and reconcile the existing shipment.
choices.why: Recovery must respect current data and side effects already committed.

completion: You can connect a failure to build scope, callback configuration or persistent release side effects without deploying.

title: Bring the service back to healthy
intro: Diagnose four local fixtures representing a Render API and worker. Every fix is a teaching decision, not a cloud change.

scenarios.title: The router cannot reach the API
evidence: Start log: listening on 127.0.0.1:3000
Configured PORT: 10000
Process has not exited
scenarios.question: Which configuration should the hosted-service fixture use?

choices.text: 0.0.0.0 and the supplied PORT.
choices.why: The platform router needs a reachable interface and configured listener; the actual course stays on localhost.

choices.text: No HTTP listener.
choices.why: A web service must receive HTTP traffic.

choices.text: A secret added to the query string.
choices.why: Credentials do not fix the listener and should not be exposed in URLs.

scenarios.title: The readiness probe gets 401
evidence: GET /health: 401
Authenticated order request: 200
Global session middleware covers every path
scenarios.question: What is the proportionate repair?

choices.text: Remove order ownership checks.
choices.why: This creates an unrelated security flaw.

choices.text: Provide the minimal dedicated probe path while preserving business authorization.
choices.why: The probe contract and customer permissions have separate purposes.

choices.text: Return 200 from checkout even when saves fail.
choices.why: This hides errors and lies about business outcomes.

scenarios.title: Invoice disappears after restart
evidence: PDF written to /tmp/invoice.pdf
Process restarted
Database still holds the path string
scenarios.question: What is missing?

choices.text: A longer filename.
choices.why: Naming does not make temporary bytes durable.

choices.text: A second browser refresh.
choices.why: The artifact is no longer present.

choices.text: Durable private storage plus an authorized database reference.
choices.why: The final bytes need persistence, while the record needs ownership and location metadata.

scenarios.title: Worker cannot reach its API
evidence: Worker and private service are in different regions
Configured address is an internal Render hostname
No supported cross-region connection was configured
scenarios.question: What should be checked?

choices.text: The actual private-network boundary and region placement.
choices.why: Internal hostnames are only useful within the supported network; design a secure reachable connection.

choices.text: Whether the database is named after the project.
choices.why: A display name cannot fix routing.

choices.text: Whether all API routes can become public and unprotected.
choices.why: Reachability must be solved without removing service authorization.

completion: You can distinguish listener, readiness, persistence and network failures using concrete evidence.

title: Place the store components
intro: Place each responsibility in the simplest appropriate zone for our chosen example: browser, trusted application server, durable data service or optional worker. All three platforms are optional choices.

sortItems.label: Display a shirt and collect quantity input
sortItems.why: Presentation and user intent belong in the browser; the submitted quantity is still untrusted.

sortItems.label: Authorize cart ownership and calculate the payable total
sortItems.why: The server uses verified identity and trusted records before an operation is accepted.

sortItems.label: Enforce stored relationships and unique fulfillment intent
sortItems.why: Database constraints protect shared facts even when multiple requests overlap.

sortItems.label: Consume a durable invoice queue with bounded concurrency
sortItems.why: A separate worker is justified when independent asynchronous execution is a requirement.

sortItems.label: Keep the shipping provider credential
sortItems.why: A server-only credential belongs to the trusted service making the provider request, never the browser.

sortItems.label: Persist orders, operation status and provider identifier mappings
sortItems.why: Durable records let the system recover after processes disappear.

scenarios.title: A small request-based store
evidence: One team
Short request handlers
No independent long-running workload
scenarios.question: What is a reasonable initial design?

choices.text: One application with server routes and managed durable data.
choices.why: This is sufficient if it meets the workload and operational requirements.

choices.text: Always require all three platforms.
choices.why: Vendor count is not an acceptance criterion.

choices.text: Browser-only checkout with a secret key.
choices.why: Trusted money and access operations cannot be delegated to an untrusted client.

scenarios.title: A new invoice workload
evidence: Large PDF generation delays responses
Jobs must survive deploys
Current system has durable order records
scenarios.question: What extra responsibility is justified?

choices.text: Move every button into another microservice.
choices.why: That does not address the specific asynchronous requirement.

choices.text: A durable job path and a worker or workflow suited to the workload.
choices.why: The separation addresses process lifetime and scaling while retaining an operation record.

choices.text: Fire an unawaited promise and return success.
choices.why: No durable work record or recovery is guaranteed.

scenarios.title: Where is the authoritative price?
evidence: Browser sends totalMinor: 1
Stored shirt price: 25000 INR minor units
Quantity: 1
scenarios.question: Which component decides the payable amount?

choices.text: The browser because the customer controls it.
choices.why: Customer input is not an authoritative price.

choices.text: Any cache entry from last year.
choices.why: Checkout must apply the current trusted pricing contract.

choices.text: The trusted business operation using validated server data.
choices.why: The architecture needs a clear pricing authority, not competing calculations.

completion: You can explain every component, its credential boundary and the requirement for any optional service.

title: Book one parcel without duplicates
intro: Follow a synthetic Fieldstore parcel through quote, booking timeout and pickup preparation. No Shiprocket request is made.

scenarios.title: Measure the packed shirt
evidence: Actual weight: 0.4 kg
Exercise-only divisor: 5000
scenarios.question: Which weight comparison is correct before courier-specific slabs?

choices.why: The assumed volumetric calculation is 3000/5000. Actual pricing still needs the selected courier rules.

choices.text: 0.4 kg, dimensions never matter.
choices.why: Space can affect chargeable weight.
Money minor units and package weights must remain distinct.

scenarios.title: Create response is lost
evidence: Fulfillment intent: FULFILLMENT_PLACEHOLDER
Provider fixture created SHIPMENT_PLACEHOLDER
Client observed a timeout
scenarios.question: What is the next state and action?

choices.text: failed; create a new order immediately.
choices.why: A timeout did not prove rejection and can lead to duplicates.

choices.text: uncertain; reconcile the existing intent and reference.
choices.why: Recover the already-created resource using supported evidence before considering a new create.

choices.text: delivered; deduct stock again.
choices.why: Neither delivery nor a second stock effect follows from a timeout.

scenarios.title: Recover the booking
evidence: Reconciliation matched account, reference and parcel
Existing provider shipment: SHIPMENT_PLACEHOLDER
No AWB assigned yet
scenarios.question: What should be saved?

choices.text: Only a green success icon.
choices.why: An icon cannot support retries or later API operations.

choices.text: A fresh merchant reference for another shipment.
choices.why: The existing resource has been confirmed.

choices.text: The provider identifiers on the existing fulfillment intent, then resume AWB assignment.
choices.why: The mapping lets later steps use the correct ID type without another booking.

scenarios.title: Pickup has not happened
evidence: AWB assigned
Label ready
Pickup requested; no collection evidence
scenarios.question: What should the customer see?

choices.text: Awaiting pickup.
choices.why: Documents and requests prepare movement; actual handover evidence is still missing.

choices.text: Delivered.
choices.why: No delivery evidence exists.

choices.text: Refund paid.
choices.why: Refund execution is a separate business operation.

completion: You recovered the same synthetic booking and distinguished its documents from physical shipment.

title: Resolve delivery, return and money separately
intro: Work through an event timeline with safe decisions. The store, provider, bank and warehouse facts remain separate.

scenarios.title: Delayed notification
evidence: Saved shipment: delivered at 14:00
Incoming event: in_transit observed 10:00
Token validated; event not yet stored
scenarios.question: How do you apply it?

choices.text: Store the observation, avoid blind regression and reconcile a contradiction.
choices.why: Arrival order is not event order; semantic transition rules protect state.

choices.text: Always overwrite with the newest arrival.
choices.why: That can regress a delivered parcel.

choices.text: Compare the numeric status codes as if they were timestamps.
choices.why: Provider codes name states, not universal progress ranks.

scenarios.title: Failed delivery becomes RTO
evidence: One failed attempt recorded
Supported return-to-origin action confirmed
Parcel has not reached the warehouse
scenarios.question: Can the item become available stock?

choices.text: Yes, immediately at the request.
choices.why: The physical item and its condition are unverified.

choices.text: No; track return, confirm receipt and inspect.
choices.why: Movement initiation is not sellable inventory.

choices.text: Yes, if the tracking webhook was authenticated.
choices.why: Authentication does not turn an intermediate event into a warehouse inspection.

scenarios.title: A damaged shirt arrives
evidence: Warehouse received one returned shirt
Inspection: damaged, not sellable
Prepaid refund request: approved but not executed
scenarios.question: What are the correct records?

choices.text: Available stock +1 and refund successful.
choices.why: Neither sellability nor money movement is supported.

choices.text: No record because damaged items do not count.
choices.why: Receipt and disposition still require an audit trail.

choices.text: Record receipt and damaged disposition; keep refund approved pending execution.
choices.why: Inventory condition and refund execution are independent facts.

scenarios.title: Delivered COD, no bank match
evidence: Order total: INR 25000 minor units
Delivery and customer collection confirmed
No remittance/bank receipt matched
scenarios.question: What should staff do?

choices.text: Keep collection confirmed and reconcile remittance and applicable adjustments.
choices.why: A courier collection event is not evidence that funds reached the merchant bank.

choices.text: Charge the customer again.
choices.why: The customer collection is already confirmed.

choices.text: Mark merchant bank receipt from tracking alone.
choices.why: Movement status cannot prove a bank transfer.

completion: You kept tracking, return inspection, refunds and COD remittance consistent without merging their states.

title: The unverified payment desk
intro: The browser, backend and provider show different clues. Decide what Fieldstore should display and do without making real payment calls.

scenarios.title: The browser celebrates first
evidence: FS-1001 expects 25000 INR minor units.
Browser callback says success; verified backend payment state is pending.
No capture evidence is stored.
scenarios.question: What should the customer and staff see?

choices.text: Pending verification; staff reconcile A-1.
choices.why: Accurate uncertainty avoids shipping or charging again without evidence.

choices.text: Paid and ready to ship.
choices.why: The browser callback alone is not verified financial evidence.

choices.text: Failed; pay again immediately.
choices.why: The existing attempt may already have succeeded.

scenarios.title: One captured event arrives twice
evidence: Provider event E-1 has a valid verified payload.
A-1 matches expected order, amount and currency.
E-1 is delivered twice; one order confirmation is already recorded.
scenarios.question: Which transition is valid?

choices.text: Confirm twice so both deliveries are acknowledged.
choices.why: Repeated delivery should not produce another allocation or notification intent.

choices.text: Record/reuse the existing event outcome and keep one effect.
choices.why: Event uniqueness plus guarded business transitions handles retries.

choices.text: Reverse the payment because the provider repeated it.
choices.why: Duplicate delivery is not evidence of a refund or reversal.

scenarios.title: Captured is not settled
evidence: A-1 is verified captured for 25000 minor units.
Settlement report has not yet matched bank evidence.
No refund was requested.
scenarios.question: What is the accurate accounting view?

choices.text: Unpaid because settlement is pending.
choices.why: This erases a verified customer payment.

choices.text: Refunded because settlement is pending.
choices.why: No refund evidence exists.

choices.text: Paid; merchant settlement pending reconciliation.
choices.why: Customer collection and merchant-bank receipt are separate dimensions.

completion: Explain pending verification, duplicate protection and settlement separately; the local panel cannot prove a live payment integration.

title: One order, one useful message
intro: Trace a repeated order event through a durable intent, a provider attempt and delivery feedback. All recipients and messages are synthetic.

scenarios.title: Five copies of one event
evidence: Five events reference order FS-1001 and receipt template v1.
Recipient customer-A and channel email are unchanged.
No receipt intent exists yet.
scenarios.question: How many business intents should be created?

choices.text: Five, because five events arrived.
choices.why: Delivery count is not business-intent count.

choices.text: One unique receipt intent with repeatable delivery work.
choices.why: A stable unique intent key prevents repeated order events from becoming repeated receipts.

choices.text: Zero; events can never be trusted.
choices.why: Verified business events should produce the intended work once.

scenarios.title: The send response is lost
evidence: Worker sent intent N-1.
No response was persisted; provider acceptance is uncertain.
The provider supports the same request key within its documented window.
scenarios.question: What should the worker preserve?

choices.text: The original intent and idempotency identity.
choices.why: Reuse the supported retry mechanism and reconcile ambiguity; do not invent a fresh message.

choices.text: A new random key and a new receipt every retry.
choices.why: That can create multiple messages for one intention.

choices.text: Only an in-memory sent flag.
choices.why: A worker restart loses in-memory evidence.

scenarios.title: A week-late event and a bounce
evidence: N-1 completed last week.
The original event is replayed after the provider dedupe window.
A separate message N-2 has a permanent bounce.
scenarios.question: Which policy handles both?

choices.text: Resend both forever until every customer complains.
choices.why: Retries do not fix a permanent destination failure and can duplicate N-1.

choices.text: Delete all notification records.
choices.why: That removes the evidence preventing repeated sends.

choices.text: Use the durable ledger for N-1; follow bounce/suppression policy for N-2.
choices.why: Application history outlives short provider keys, and delivery failures need their own resolution.

completion: Show one intent for repeated events and distinguish retry, deliberate resend, acceptance and delivery.

title: Find the failing boundary
intro: Compare browser and server evidence before changing security configuration. Diagnose each local scenario and preserve the permission rules.

scenarios.title: Works in an API client
evidence: API client receives 200 from an owned-order request.
Browser UI uses port 3000; API uses port 4000.
OPTIONS lacks the intended Allow-Origin response.
scenarios.question: What should be investigated first?

choices.text: The origin/preflight response for the intended UI.
choices.why: A browser-only read boundary can fail even when the handler works for an API client.

choices.text: Remove all session verification.
choices.why: That changes authorization, not the missing CORS response.

choices.text: Put the API secret into the browser.
choices.why: Secrets do not belong in client requests and do not repair CORS.

scenarios.title: CORS is fixed, ownership is not granted
evidence: Preflight now succeeds.
Customer-A requests customer-B order.
Server returns 403 and no private payload.
scenarios.question: What does this show?

choices.text: CORS is still broken and all origins must be allowed.
choices.why: A 403 from the handler can be an intentional authorization result.

choices.text: The ownership boundary is correctly denying this request.
choices.why: Use an owned resource for the successful case; preserve cross-account rejection.

choices.text: The order ID should replace the login session.
choices.why: A resource identifier is not authentication.

scenarios.title: No callback reaches localhost
evidence: The local course opens at 127.0.0.1:3000.
An external provider cannot reach that machine through loopback.
The course must remain local and no live account is connected.
scenarios.question: Which exercise is appropriate now?

choices.text: Disable TLS checks and publish credentials.
choices.why: That neither creates valid reachability nor preserves security.

choices.text: Expose the whole course automatically.
choices.why: The task explicitly excludes hosting and live connections.

choices.text: Use local signed fixtures and document optional supported callback setup.
choices.why: Fixtures teach verification safely; live reachability remains a separate optional check.

completion: Separate DNS/TLS, browser CORS and application authorization; never weaken one boundary to conceal another.

title: Recover the morning backlog
intro: A synthetic incident crosses workers, payments and recovery records. Choose the evidence and repairs that preserve business history.

scenarios.title: The queue grows after a credential expires
evidence: Oldest shipment job age is rising.
Worker logs show provider-authentication failures after rotation.
Repeated retries create no successful external results.
scenarios.question: What is the targeted first repair?

choices.text: Restore the approved credential reference, validate it safely, and resume bounded work.
choices.why: Fix authentication while preserving queued intent IDs and evidence.

choices.text: Create a new shipment intent for every retry.
choices.why: That can duplicate bookings once authentication is restored.

choices.text: Drop the backlog so the graph looks healthy.
choices.why: Deleting pending work hides unfulfilled orders.

scenarios.title: Connections are exhausted
evidence: Worker concurrency increased from 4 to 40.
Database activity shows many waiting connections and long transactions.
Checkout latency rose at the same time.
scenarios.question: Which response addresses the evidence?

choices.text: Increase all retries immediately.
choices.why: That amplifies pressure on the constrained resource.

choices.text: Bound concurrency and investigate transaction/connection lifetimes.
choices.why: Release resources correctly, then verify recovery with a small replay sample.

choices.text: Assume every slow request is a cache problem.
choices.why: The observed connection evidence deserves investigation first.

scenarios.title: Restore meets a captured payment
evidence: Isolated restored database says FS-1001 unpaid.
Provider evidence shows A-1 captured before the outage.
Outbound effects remain disabled during recovery.
scenarios.question: What must happen before reopening?

choices.text: Charge again from restored data.
choices.why: Restoration does not erase external money movement.

choices.text: Discard provider evidence.
choices.why: That creates a false history.

choices.text: Reconcile A-1, rebuild/review local records and verify invariants.
choices.why: Stable references connect recovery data to external reality without duplicate effects.

completion: Describe the root cause, controlled repair, replay gate and evidence that confirms recovery—not merely an empty queue.

title: Fieldstore: one complete purchase
intro: Follow customer-A through ten connected stages. Start with one sellable blue shirt at 25000 INR minor units, onHand 1 and reserved 0. Shipping is free and tax is included only for this synthetic exercise. Every decision preserves an evidence trail.

scenarios.title: 01 · Signup and verified identity
evidence: A signup form returns a visible success message.
The session fixture has expired.
Profile metadata contains a user-edited role=admin.
scenarios.question: Which identity may the server rely on?

choices.text: The editable profile role.
choices.why: User-controlled metadata cannot grant staff permission.

choices.text: A currently verified session and separately controlled permissions.
choices.why: Reauthenticate or refresh through the supported auth flow; derive authority from trusted records.

choices.text: The success animation.
choices.why: A screen animation is not credential verification.

scenarios.data: Reads session evidence; creates/loads a customer identity. Staff role data is separately controlled.
scenarios.rule: Verify current identity; never grant authority from user-editable profile fields.
scenarios.service: Synthetic auth adapter; optional real auth provider requires separate testing.
scenarios.failure: Expired session or forged admin metadata.
scenarios.verify: Use expired and valid fixtures; confirm only the valid customer identity continues and no staff role is granted.

scenarios.title: 02 · Product and authoritative price
evidence: Variant shirt-blue-M is active.
Trusted unit price is 25000 INR minor units.
Browser text is edited to show a price of 1.
scenarios.question: Which price defines the purchase?

choices.text: The trusted active variant price, rechecked during checkout.
choices.why: The display can change independently; authoritative records define the quote.

choices.text: The browser text because the customer can see it.
choices.why: Visible client text is untrusted input.

choices.text: A random price copied from another cart.
choices.why: Quotes need the chosen variant and current business rules.

scenarios.actor: Catalog read handler and customer browser.
scenarios.data: Reads approved product/variant fields and trusted unit price; exposes public catalog data.
scenarios.rule: Only approved catalog fields are public; browser pricing never becomes authoritative.
scenarios.service: Synthetic catalog/database records; product-image storage is separate.
scenarios.failure: Stale display or a tampered browser price.
scenarios.verify: Change the displayed price and confirm the server quote still uses 25000 minor units.

scenarios.title: 03 · Cart ownership and persistence
evidence: Customer-B is authenticated.
The submitted cart ID is cart-A.
Cart-A belongs to customer-A and has one shirt.
scenarios.question: What should Add to cart do?

choices.text: Accept because both customers have accounts.
choices.why: Authentication does not imply access to another customer’s cart.

choices.text: Reveal cart-A details to explain the rejection.
choices.why: A rejection should not disclose private cart contents.

choices.text: Reject B without changing cart-A; allow A and verify after reload.
choices.why: The resource owner must be checked before mutation.

scenarios.actor: Cart Route Handler using verified customer identity.
scenarios.data: Reads cart owner and variant; writes cart_items only for an authorized cart.
scenarios.rule: Quantity is validated; ownership is enforced on the server; cart addition does not reserve stock in this model.
scenarios.service: Synthetic cart database; no external provider is needed.
scenarios.failure: Cross-customer cart ID or a browser-only unsaved update.
scenarios.verify: Compare B’s denied request with A’s successful persisted change and a reload.

scenarios.title: 04 · Checkout and the last unit
evidence: onHand=1, reserved=0, available=1.
A and B submit checkout for the last shirt.
Each request has a different logical checkout ID.
scenarios.question: Which stock outcome is correct?

choices.text: One atomic reservation succeeds; the other receives unavailable.
choices.why: A conditional transactional claim prevents both checkouts from consuming the same availability.

choices.text: Both reserve because each first read available=1.
choices.why: Separate read and write operations can oversell.

choices.text: Reserve twice and repair inventory after payment.
choices.why: That lets money collection outrun a broken stock promise.

scenarios.actor: Checkout service and transactional inventory boundary.
scenarios.data: Reads owned cart/current quote; writes one order intent, reservation and payment-attempt identity.
scenarios.rule: Availability never becomes negative; only one claimant gets the last unit; quote is 25000 INR minor units.
scenarios.service: Synthetic database transaction model; provider payment work follows the protected intent.
scenarios.failure: Concurrent last-unit requests or repeated checkout clicks.
scenarios.verify: Observe exactly one reservation, reserved 1/available 0, and a safe unavailable response for the other customer.

scenarios.title: 05 · Payment and duplicate verification
evidence: A’s browser reports success.
A-1 initially remains pending verification.
A valid captured event matching 25000 INR arrives twice.
scenarios.question: Which effect is allowed?

choices.text: Ship from the browser callback before verification.
choices.why: The browser alone cannot confirm trusted payment state.

choices.text: Apply one verified capture and keep one allocation.
choices.why: Authenticate and match evidence, then use guarded transitions and event identity to handle duplicates.

choices.text: Allocate twice because two events arrived.
choices.why: Delivery duplication must not duplicate inventory or order effects.

scenarios.actor: Payment adapter, webhook handler and reconciliation worker.
scenarios.data: Reads A-1 expected references; stores event evidence and the verified payment transition.
scenarios.rule: Match amount, currency and order; one logical payment effect; physical stock is not deducted at capture.
scenarios.service: Synthetic Razorpay-shaped fixture, not a real transaction or SDK invocation.
scenarios.failure: Delayed verification, wrong signature, replayed captured event or late failure.
scenarios.verify: Show pending-verification first, then one captured result; replay leaves onHand 1/reserved 1 unchanged.

scenarios.title: 06 · Order confirmation and private access
evidence: FS-1001 has a purchased-item snapshot and verified payment.
Customer-B requests FS-1001.
One order-confirmed outbox entry already exists.
scenarios.question: What does the order service do?

choices.text: Expose it because the payment is complete.
choices.why: Paid orders still contain private customer information.

choices.text: Create another order and outbox event for B.
choices.why: That breaks ownership and duplicates business work.

choices.text: Deny B; let A read the saved snapshot and keep one confirmation intent.
choices.why: Order privacy and duplicate-safe downstream work remain required after payment.

scenarios.actor: Order service, authenticated customer view and authorized staff view.
scenarios.data: Reads order ownership; preserves item/price snapshot and one downstream work record.
scenarios.rule: Only permitted actors read the order; catalog edits cannot rewrite purchased history.
scenarios.service: Synthetic database/outbox; notification and shipment adapters consume saved work.
scenarios.failure: Unauthorized order access or a repeated confirmation event.
scenarios.verify: Compare A/B access and count one order confirmation and one notification/shipment intent.

scenarios.title: 07 · Shipment booking and physical handoff
evidence: First provider attempt returns 401 after credential expiry.
After credential repair, booking times out; provider fixture shows shipment S-1 for FS-1001.
No physical pickup/handoff has happened yet.
scenarios.question: Which recovery protects the order?

choices.text: Refresh supported credentials, reconcile/link S-1, and wait for handoff evidence.
choices.why: Authentication failure and uncertain booking need distinct repairs; neither proves physical shipment.

choices.text: Create a new shipment after every timeout.
choices.why: S-1 already exists and a blind retry can book a duplicate.

choices.text: Deduct stock twice because booking and label are separate actions.
choices.why: The allocation is consumed once at the agreed physical handoff.

scenarios.actor: Authorized fulfillment worker and shipping adapter.
scenarios.data: Reads order/address/package snapshot; stores provider shipment/AWB references and booking evidence.
scenarios.rule: One booking intent per fulfillment; protect credentials; booking is separate from physical stock consumption.
scenarios.service: Synthetic shipping-provider fixture; use documented Shiprocket behavior in an optional integration.
scenarios.failure: Expired credentials and a response lost after provider booking.
scenarios.verify: Count one matched shipment; at later confirmed handoff change onHand 1/reserved 1 to onHand 0/reserved 0 exactly once.

scenarios.title: 08 · Tracking and delivery evidence
evidence: Verified mapped tracking says delivered.
An older in-transit event arrives later.
Payment remains captured; settlement is a separate record.
scenarios.question: How should the timeline change?

choices.text: Regress the shipment to in transit because it arrived last.
choices.why: Arrival order is not event time or valid state progression.

choices.text: Retain delivered and record the stale event as evidence without regression.
choices.why: Map the provider status and event timing through allowed transitions.

choices.text: Mark payment settled because the parcel is delivered.
choices.why: Delivery and bank settlement are independent facts.

scenarios.actor: Tracking event intake and reconciliation job.
scenarios.data: Stores original provider event and mapped internal shipment status; reads existing transition history.
scenarios.rule: Authenticate using the provider’s actual scheme; handle duplicates, delay and missing events deliberately.
scenarios.service: Synthetic courier/aggregator tracking feed; no universal signature or sandbox is assumed.
scenarios.failure: Out-of-order, duplicated or absent tracking notifications.
scenarios.verify: Apply the stale event and confirm delivery does not regress; demonstrate a reconciliation lookup for missing evidence.

scenarios.title: 09 · Return, quarantine and inspection
evidence: A requests return of the delivered shirt.
The return is authorized and then physically received.
Inspection finds it sellable.
scenarios.question: When may available inventory increase?

choices.text: When A first clicks Return.
choices.why: A request does not prove the item was received or is sellable.

choices.text: When any reverse-pickup label is printed.
choices.why: A label does not prove physical condition.

choices.text: After receipt and a recorded sellable inspection under policy.
choices.why: Quarantine separates received goods from sellable stock; record the restock exactly once.

scenarios.actor: Customer return request, authorized staff and warehouse inspection.
scenarios.data: Writes return authorization, reverse-fulfillment references, received/quarantine evidence and inspection result.
scenarios.rule: Return ownership and policy apply; sellable stock increases only after suitable inspection, not automatically on refund.
scenarios.failure: Unauthorized return, lost reverse parcel, damaged item or duplicate inspection event.
scenarios.verify: Before inspection available stays 0; after sellable inspection, one guarded restock transfers the unit from quarantine to onHand 1/reserved 0/available 1.

scenarios.title: 10 · Refund and final reconciliation
evidence: Captured amount is 25000 INR minor units.
Authorized staff approve refund R-1 for 25000.
Provider accepts R-1, but final processed evidence has not arrived.
scenarios.question: What should the final board show now?

choices.text: Refund pending with its own reference; reconcile before another refund.
choices.why: Acceptance is not confirmed completion; keep payment, stock and refund histories separate.

choices.text: Refund completed and bank transfer guaranteed immediately.
choices.why: The current evidence does not establish that result.

choices.text: Create R-2 to speed up the pending refund.
choices.why: A duplicate monetary intent can exceed the approved amount.

scenarios.actor: Authorized refund service, provider adapter and finance reconciliation.
scenarios.data: Reads captured/refunded totals; writes a bounded refund intent, provider reference and final evidence when known.
scenarios.rule: Refund authority and cumulative amount checks are atomic; uncertainty must not trigger a fresh duplicate refund.
scenarios.service: Synthetic Razorpay-shaped refund and settlement fixtures.
scenarios.failure: Unauthorized refund request, double click, timeout or missing final refund event.
scenarios.verify: Reject unauthorized and excessive requests; apply processed evidence once and reconcile money, stock and order history separately.

completion: Complete all ten decisions and explain the actor, records, permission, service, failure and verification at every handoff. The evidence proves the synthetic model, not a live store.
